extracted.intended_audience: theologians, students of Catholic dogmatic theology, clergy, and scholars of patristics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes doctrinal standards and canonical propositions concerning grace, justification, faith, prayer, merit, and the necessity of divine aid as presented in patristic, conciliar, and scholastic texts and condemnations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief must rest on divine authority of revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conc. Vat., Sess. III, De Fide, can. 2: “Si quis dixerit, ... ad fidem divinam non requiri, ut revelata veritas propter auctoritatem Dei revelantis credatur, anathema sit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The canon condemns any opinion that revealed truth need not be believed because of the authority of God revealing it. The surrounding discussion references defenders of contrary opinions and advises consulting secondary literature (e.g., Schiffini, Palmieri, Scheeben). Anti‑pattern: treating revelation as credible on purely natural or creaturely grounds without appeal to divine authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevenient inspiration/aid of the Holy Spirit required for true faith and acts leading to justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sess. VI can. 3: “Si quis dixerit, sine praeveniente Spiritus Sancti inspiratione atque eius adiutorio hominem credere, sperare, diligere aut poenitere posse, ... anathema sit.” (Denzinger-Bannwart, n. 813.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal standard: the initial acts (faith, hope, charity, penance) that dispose to justification cannot rightly be ascribed to mere natural effort apart from the Spirit’s prior illumination and aid. The text cites Arausican canons and patristic/scholastic explanations (Suarez, Augustine). Anti‑pattern: claiming faith can arise solely from natural powers without divine assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace is not merely an aid making moral action easier; it is necessary for right action to attain eternal life
rubrics_metrics.description: Sess. VI can. 2: condemnation of saying grace is given only so that a man may more easily fulfill the command, as if man could do both without grace (Denzinger-Bannwart, n. 812).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that grace is required, not merely facilitative. The text draws on John XV, Augustine, and scholastics (Molina, Bellarmine, Thomassin, Ruiz) to argue that supernatural virtue required for eternal life exceeds natural powers. Anti‑pattern: treating grace as non‑essential or merely a superadded convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works done before justification are not to be called truly sins in themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Conc. Trid., Sess. VI, can. 7: “Si quis dixerit, opera omnia, quae ante iustificationem fiunt, ... vere esse peccata, ... anathema sit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine standard rejects the blanket claim that every action before justification is truly a sin. The passage is cited amid debates on the status of pre‑justification acts. Anti‑pattern: asserting indiscriminately that all pre‑justification actions are morally sinful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the doctrine that in man without grace all his actions are corrupted and therefore sinful
rubrics_metrics.description: Denzinger-Bannwart n. 1523 condemns the synodal doctrine that a man without grace, under the dominion of concupiscence, has all his actions infected and corrupted so that all his works before justification are sins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condemned proposition is identified as false and pernicious and is denounced as leading to error. The guidance points readers to Tridentine and Baiusan condemnations. Anti‑pattern: reducing every human act under concupiscence to total sinfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: God hears the prayer of sinners; not everything said about God’s non‑hearing of sinners is absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural and patristic debate: statements like “Scimus autem quia peccatores Deus non audit” are balanced by patristic texts (Tract. in Ioa., 44) arguing that God does hear sinners (e.g., the publican in Luke XVIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page discusses divergent patristic readings and Suarez/Faure commentaries to clarify context; it warns against absolutizing texts to deny that God may hear or answer repenting sinners. Anti‑pattern: using a scriptural phrase out of context to assert God never listens to sinners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is a gift of God (non ex vobis / Dei donum), not merely an act originating in us
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple citations (Eph. II, 8; ‘Non ex vobis’; Denzinger canons; Augustine and Suarez): faith’s beginning and supplement are from God, not from unaided human initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites councils and patristic testimony to assert that faith’s origin is divine. Scholastic treatments (Suarez, Palmieri) explicate this. Anti‑pattern: claiming faith originates purely from human faculties or that faith is entirely a human acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human acts performed without charity (caritas) are not truly good works meriting virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: De Gratia Christi c. 26 and De Gratia et Libero Arbitrio c. 18: statements such as “Ubi non est dilectio, nullum bonum opus imputatur” and that actions done without charity are not rightly called good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral appraisal requires charity: even apparently good external acts, if done without love, are not truly good in the theological sense. Use this as a criterion to evaluate moral quality of acts. Anti‑pattern: treating external conformity or natural benevolence as equivalent to supernatural charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer is both testimony of grace and a means by which God bestows faith and perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: Patristic and conciliar texts (e.g., Ep. 177: “Oratio est clarissima gratiae testificatio”; Arausic. II; De Dono Perseverantiae) assert prayer’s role in eliciting and securing divine gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page treats prayer as instrumentally efficacious: Churches and pastors are admonished to pray for unbelievers and the faithful, as prayer precedes and secures divine movement. Suarez and others discuss the relation between petition and divine promise. Anti‑pattern: denying any causal or instrumental role of prayer in conversion/perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance is a divine gift that must be sought in prayer and is distinct from confirmatio in gratia
rubrics_metrics.description: De Dono Perseverantiae (and Suarez, De Gratia XII, 38): perseverance is to be asked for in prayer, is a special donum, and must not be conflated with confirmation in grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perseverantia is described as requiring continual petition and moral dispositions; scholastics articulate conditions and differences from other graces. Anti‑pattern: presuming perseverance as an automatic result of initial justification or merging it with other graces.

rubrics_metrics.name: No one can come to Christ unless drawn by the Father (necessity of divine drawing)
rubrics_metrics.description: John VI, 44 cited: “Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit (ἐλκύσῃ) eum.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to support doctrines of divine initiative in conversion; the text references patristic and scholastic exegesis (Schiffini, etc.). Anti‑pattern: interpreting this passage to deny human responsibility entirely; rather, it emphasizes divine antecedent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace is necessary for meriting eternal life; natural operations cannot produce meritorious works proportionate to eternal life
rubrics_metrics.description: Summa Theol., 1a 2ae, q.109, a.5: 'Vita aeterna est finis excedens proportionem naturae humanae ... et ideo homo per sua naturalia non potest producere opera meritoria proportionata vitae aeternae; sed ad hoc exigitur altior virtus, quae est virtus gratiae.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological criterion for merit: supernatural virtue (grace) is required to produce meritable acts for eternal reward. The text points readers to Augustine, Thomistic treatments, and modern commentators. Anti‑pattern: conflating natural moral goodness with meritorious supernatural merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is false and presumptuous to claim one is without sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural and patristic admonitions (1 John I, 8; Augustine: 'Nemo itaque dicat, se esse sine peccato') warn against claiming sinlessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for pastoral/moral humility: even saints acknowledge failures; claiming perfect sinlessness is delusive. The text references exegetical debate about ‘no sin’ statements and cites Augustine’s counsel to hate sin while recognizing personal frailty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special privileges (e.g., Blessed Virgin’s immunity from all venial sins) are exceptional and defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Sess. VI, can. 23: condemns saying a justified person in ordinary life can avoid all venial sins except by special privilege such as that held for the Blessed Virgin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges the unique, defined privilege of Mary while denying that the ordinary justified state entails absolute freedom from venial fault without special divine favor. Use this to evaluate claims about universal sanctity or sinlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit defined as recompense: merit and reward are fittingly understood in justice
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Thomas (Summa Theol., cited): 'Meritum et merces ad idem referuntur... recompensare mercedem operis vel laboris est actus iustitiae.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scholastic account treats merit as a just recompense due for certain acts when infused virtue is present; consult Taparelli and other moral theologians for development. Anti‑pattern: misunderstanding merit as purely natural or denying its relation to divine justice and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human nature retains form, life, reason etc. after the fall, but lacks true perception of supernatural good without grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Contr. Collat., n. 36: 'Naturae humanae, cuius creator est Deus, etiam post praevaricationem manet substantia, manet forma, manet vita et sensus et ratio ceteraque corporis et animi bona, quae etiam malis vitiosisque non desunt. Sed non illis veri boni perceptio est...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion distinguishes preserved natural faculties from the supernatural perception and reception of true good; theological evaluation should avoid denying the continued existence of natural goods while affirming their insufficiency for supernatural ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish human licit love from divine charity; human affections may be licit though imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: Serm. de Temp. and related texts: 'Caritas alia est divina, alia humana; alia est humana licita, alia illicita.... Licitam ergo caritatem habete; humana est, sed ut dixi licita.... Liceat vobis humanâ caritate diligere coniuges, diligere filios, diligere amicos.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral/moral criterion: not all human affection is blameworthy; some human loves are licit and even necessary. Theological judgment must separate lawful human affections from illicit attachments contrary to charity.
